name: HeyClicky
tagline: Desktop app that plays mechanical keyboard switch sounds as you type on whatever keyboard you actually own.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The whole product is three parts: a global keystroke listener, a bank of short audio samples, and an audio path fast enough that the click lands with the finger. An agent can wire all three in an afternoon on any desktop OS, and the result is genuinely usable. What it will not hand you is the sample library, which is the part that took someone a microphone, a stack of switches, and patience. If you can live with free or self recorded samples, the DIY version is the same product. If you want a signed tray app that sounds like a lubed Holy Panda, you are buying recordings, not code.
coreLoopDIY: Listens for global key press and release events and fires a preloaded short sample per key with near zero latency, with a tray toggle and volume control.
requirements: WAV samples you recorded or licensed yourself
macOS Input Monitoring / Accessibility permission, or equivalent on Linux
whatYouLose: Professionally recorded, level matched sample packs for specific switches
Per key and per modifier sampling so space and enter do not sound like the letter J
Latency tuning that someone already fought with on a dozen audio setups
A signed, notarized app that does not trip OS security warnings or need a terminal
Whatever extras ship with it: presets, hotkeys, updates, sane defaults
moatNotes: Sample recordings are the actual asset here. Code is a weekend, a clean set of switch recordings is not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants to build a global keyboard hook, grant it scary system permissions, and then go hunting for clean switch recordings that are legal to use, all to get a sound they can have for the price of a sandwich. Low priced utilities like this win on the gap between five minutes and five hours. The DIY build is real and it works, it just costs an evening and sounds worse until you find better samples.
notes: A keystroke listener plus a sample player is one of the shortest paths from empty folder to working app that still feels like magic.
prompt:
Build a local desktop app called clacker that plays mechanical keyboard sounds as I type.

Stack: Python 3.11, pynput for global keyboard events, sounddevice plus soundfile plus numpy for audio, pystray plus Pillow for a tray icon. No Electron, no web UI, no server.

Behavior:
- On start, load every WAV in ./packs/PACKNAME/ into memory as float32 numpy arrays at a single shared samplerate, resampling on load if needed.
- Open one persistent sounddevice OutputStream with a small blocksize and mix samples into the callback. Never open a new stream per keystroke.
- On key press, pick the sample mapped to that key from mapping.json; fall back to a round robin of generic press samples. On key release, play a release sample if one exists.
- Support overlapping sounds: keep a list of active voices in the mix callback, drop finished ones.
- Randomize gain by plus or minus 1.5 dB per hit so fast typing does not sound like a machine gun.
- Tray menu: enable/disable, volume 25/50/75/100 percent, pick pack from the folders present, quit.
- Config in config.json next to the script: pack name, volume, enabled. Write on change, read on start.

In scope: global listening while any app is focused, per key mapping, multiple packs, tray control, low latency.
Out of scope: accounts, telemetry, cloud sync, auto update, app store packaging, bundled sample packs.

Ship a packs/README.md explaining that I must supply my own WAV files and that samples should be short, trimmed, and mono. Include a tiny generated placeholder click WAV so the app runs before I add anything.

Print clear setup notes in README.md, including that macOS requires Input Monitoring permission for the terminal or the built binary, and that Wayland may block global key capture. No secrets needed; if any are ever added, use .env and never commit it.
